nodes.summary: Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of positive integers with $a_n^2 / a_{n+1} \le 2/3$ for all $n$ and $\sum_n 1 / a_n = (5 - \sqrt 5) / 2$. Then $a_n = F_{2^{n+1}}$ for all $n \ge 0$, where $F_k$ is the $k$-th Fibonacci number ($F_0 = 0$, $F_1 = 1$); that is, $a$ is the sequence $F_2, F_4, F_8, \ldots$.

nodes.summary: Let $\beta \ge 0$ and $r$ be real numbers, and let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of positive integers with $|a_n^2 / a_{n+1} - \beta| \le 1/3$ for all $n$ and $\sum_n 1 / a_n = r$. Write $x_n = r - \sum_{k\lt n} 1 / a_k$. Then for every $n$ with $a_n \ge 8 (\beta + 1/3)^2$ we have $a_n = \lfloor x_n^{-1} + \beta + 1/2 \rfloor$, that is, $a_n$ is the integer nearest to $x_n^{-1} + \beta$, with halves rounded up.…

nodes.summary: Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of positive integers with $2/3 \le a_n^2 / a_{n+1} \le 4/3$ for all $n$ and $\sum_n 1 / a_n = 1$. Then $a_n = s_n(1)$ for all $n \ge 0$, where $(s_n(1))_{n \ge 0}$ is the generalized Sylvester sequence with parameter $1$, that is, the Sylvester sequence $2, 3, 7, 43, \ldots$.

nodes.summary: Let $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ be a sequence of positive integers with $a_n^2 / a_{n+1} \to 1$ such that $\sum_n 1 / a_n$ converges. Then there is a natural number $N$ such that, with $r = \sum_{k \ge 0} 1 / a_{N+k}$, the tail $(a_{N+n})_{n \ge 0}$ is the pseudo-greedy expansion of $r$, and the gap sequence of this expansion tends to $0$.

nodes.summary: For every real number $r > 0$, the pseudo-greedy expansion $(a_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of $r$ satisfies $\sum_n 1 / a_n = r$.

nodes.title: Recursion for the pseudo-greedy expansion

nodes.summary: Let $r$ be a real number with pseudo-greedy remainder sequence $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$. The pseudo-greedy expansion of $r$ is the integer sequence $a_n = \lfloor x_n^{-1} + 1 + 1/2 \rfloor$ for $n \ge 0$; that is, $a_n$ is the integer nearest to $x_n^{-1} + 1$, with halves rounded up.
nodes.title: Pseudo-greedy expansion

nodes.summary: The first term $\varepsilon_0$ of the gap sequence of the pseudo-greedy expansion of $1$ is $0$: the first remainder is $x_0 = 1$ and the first term of the expansion is $a_0 = 2$, so $\varepsilon_0 = x_0^{-1} + 1 - a_0 = 1 + 1 - 2 = 0$.
nodes.title: The first gap of the expansion of 1 vanishes

nodes.summary: Let $r > 0$ be a real number and let $(\varepsilon_n)$ be the gap sequence of its pseudo-greedy expansion. For every $n \ge 0$, if $\varepsilon_n = 0$, then $\varepsilon_{n+1} = 0$.
nodes.title: A vanishing gap stays zero

nodes.summary: Let $r$ be a real number, and let $(x_n)$ be the remainder sequence and $(a_n)$ the pseudo-greedy expansion of $r$. The gap sequence of $r$ is the real sequence $\varepsilon_n = x_n^{-1} + 1 - a_n$ for $n \ge 0$.
nodes.title: Gap sequence of the pseudo-greedy expansion

nodes.summary: For every real number $r$ and every $n \ge 0$, the remainder sequence $(x_n)$ and the pseudo-greedy expansion $(a_n)$ of $r$ satisfy $x_{n+1} = x_n - 1/a_n$.
nodes.title: Remainder recursion

nodes.summary: For a real number $r$, the remainder sequence $(x_n)_{n \ge 0}$ of the pseudo-greedy expansion of $r$ is defined by $x_0 = r$ and $x_{n+1} = x_n - 1/a_n$, where $a_n = \lfloor x_n^{-1} + 1 + 1/2 \rfloor$ is the integer nearest to $x_n^{-1} + 1$, with halves rounded up.
